subject: Cognitive Science
title: Distributed Cognition
description: A short lesson to help you apply Distributed Cognition.

hook.text: A pilot, copilot, and instruments together land the plane. No single mind holds all the knowledge.

buildup.text: Distributed cognition says thinking isn't just in your head—it's spread across people and tools.

discovery.text: Edwin Hutchins studied ship navigation: the cognitive task is shared among crew and instruments.

twist.text: Your phone is part of your cognitive system. Offloading memory to it changes how your brain works.

climax.text: In modern work, individual genius matters less than how well knowledge flows through teams and tools.

punchline.text: Thinking happens between minds, not just in them.

quiz.question: What is distributed cognition?
options: Thinking spread across people, tools, and environments

details.summary: Distributed cognition proposes that thinking is not confined to individual brains but is spread across people, tools, and environments. A cockpit crew, their instruments, and checklists form a cognitive system. Writing extends memory; calculators extend computation.
details.whyItMatters: Distributed cognition challenges the myth of the solitary thinker. In practice, cognition is always scaffolded by tools, environments, and other people.
takeaways: Cognition extends across people, tools, and environments
External resources like notes and tools are part of thinking
Team intelligence emerges from distributed cognitive systems

faq.question: How is a cockpit an example of distributed cognition?
faq.answer: No single pilot holds all the information needed to fly. Knowledge is distributed across crew members, instruments, checklists, and procedures. Speed is displayed on gauges, protocol is in manuals, and altitude is called out verbally. The cognitive system is the entire cockpit, not any individual.

faq.question: Does your smartphone make you smarter?
faq.answer: In a distributed cognition framework, yes. Your phone extends memory, computation, and access to information. However, offloading too much may weaken internal cognitive skills. The relationship is complementary: tools enhance capability but also create dependency.
